entry.title: ‘Clayface’ Review: A Gross Miscalculation (Emphasis on the Gross)
entry.summary: James Watkins' gory, goopy R-rated body horror is an offbeat addition to the DCU's increasingly erratic output.
entry.content:
Three films into its latest “chapter” (this one subtitled “Gods and Monsters”), James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DCU can’t be faulted for making interesting choices. Hell, at least they’re making choices at all. Kicking off their incarnation of the latest run of comic book movies with “Superman” was unquestionably smart (it’s Superman! you know him!), even if its follow-up “Supergirl” was destined to divide audiences (even if this critic quite liked it, surely there are other reasons why some members of this seemingly dedicated audience didn’t, no matter its quality).

Enter: “Clayface.” Another set of execs and filmmakers wouldn’t have bellied up to this grim, gross anti-hero to round out their first trio of movies meant to reset a massive franchise. But does that kind of ambition and vision pay off in James Watkins‘ goopy, gory, decidedly R-rated body horror feature? Not so much, even as open-minded audiences will likely admire the big swings on offer here. It’s certainly different, and for comic book movie fans absolutely bored to death by the same old stuff, it’s something of a respite. Yet, divorced from all that, Watkins’ film confounds much more than it compels.

Related Stories
Japanese Cult Blockbuster ‘Rex: A Dinosaur’s Story’ to Get First U.S. Theatrical Release in December
Watch Ava Duvernay Explain Why the 14th Amendment Is So Much More Than Birthright Citizenship

A working knowledge of Clayface lore is not required to understand the film — the script from Mike Flangan and Hossein Amini lays out the essentials with ease, before collapsing in the film’s second half — though it’s perhaps helpful to know that that he’s always been imagined as a Batman adversary. Fair enough. Those bones of the story (bones! those will soon be in short supply!) hint at perhaps why he was chosen for this early story in the new DCU: get some Batman winks in there, introduce us to Gotham City, toy with some dark underbelly stuff.

Flanagan and Amini also latch on to another bit of early Clayface backstory: he’s an actor, a pretty natty way to make horrific facial scarring really hurt. Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries, very good at conveying genuine pathos under gobs of makeup and VFX) is a Gotham City native, a wrong-side-of-the-tracks kid who is on the cusp of superstardom. When we first meet him, he’s about to be nominated for a major award (on-screen graphics don’t say what it is, though someone later calls it an Academy Award, sure), fielding great new offers, and trying to stay grounded. His best pal Corey (Joshua James) helps, as do his frequent mentions of his fraught early life.

Matt is, by all accounts, a nice guy. He introduces himself to the pretty flight attendant on the private jet! He’s sweet to his agent! He goes back home to Gotham to chat with other rising young performers! But Matt is also — and this is something the film can never quite square — a bit too easily swayed by a pretty face and a night out at the club. When an alluring young lady (Joana Ribeiro) makes eyes at him across the dance floor, he can’t resist (even when she tells him she’s an aspiring actor; run, dude!). Thank goodness Corey is on hand to remind Matt that his new paramour is the girlfriend of local mob boss Markos Szabo (David Dencik). Too bad that Matt just doesn’t care.

Well, that’s life in Gotham City (perpetually damp, grimy, and graffiti-covered), and when Matt and Mia wake up the next morning, they’re surrounded by Markos and his band of (lightly Dick Tracy-coded) toughs. Markos, understandably ticked off (and somehow aware that Corey had told Matt that Mia was taken), takes out all his toxic masculine rage on Matt’s gorgeous face, carving him up and leaving him to deal with it. Gross, goopy, gory, bloody, and just plain meaty, Matt’s physical ailments aren’t shied away from at all, and Watkins’ dedication to going full body horror is admirable.

And the attendant facial disfigurations are bad enough (remember, Matt is an actor, he really needs his face), but what follows is arguably worse. Believing he might find justice (in Gotham City?!), Matt tries to take legal action against Markos. What follows: character assassinations, horrific surgeries, financial lootings, and the total decimation of life as he knows it. Which is all to say, when Matt meets Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie), he’s willing to do anything to get a slice of his life back. And Caitlyn sure loves slicing, dicing, and toying with “nanocells” (not clay, sorry) that Matt believes can fix his visage.

Great news! It does! Well, for a time. Hellbent on getting his life back (via his face), Matt overdoses on those damn nanocells and promptly becomes a monster, both figuratively and literally. Gone is our sweet young actor, instead replaced by a snarling, revenge-obsessed freak who is scared (and then delighted) to discover he can shift his face into whatever he wants, whoever he wants, whenever he wants. (A subplot about how Caitlyn can calm him feels terribly shoehorned in to add an icky romance dimension.)

Increasingly muddy effects and plotting don’t do Matt’s transformations many favors — the film does much better, clever work when he’s just slipping between different faces, zipping behind a door and emerging as someone else. The mechanics of those transformations aren’t clear either: are they subconscious? does he need to think of someone to “become” them? touch them? can he make their clothes too? or is that also skin? We’re spinning out just thinking on it. At least these moments allow some supporting stars, including Eddie Marsan and James, the chance to have quite a bit of fun playing Matt “playing” their characters.

A few meaty set pieces help, too, including a truly stomach-churning sequence set on an airplane (turbulence and nanocells are a bad mix) and a third act revenge-driven visit to the club that gives Rhys Harries plenty to chew on (to say nothing of some of Matt’s biggest foes). But the uneven nature of the film, its plotting, its character motivations, and its aims only become bigger and bloodier as the film winds on. Malleable, sure, but this ambitious misfire can never conform to one shape, one final form, or one good idea.

Grade: C+

Warner Bros. will release “Clayface” in theaters on Friday, October 23.

entry.title: Tom Cruise to Be Honored with AFI Life Achievement Award
entry.summary: Tom Cruise has been named as the recipient of the 52nd Life Achievement Award from the American Film Institute.
entry.content:
Tom Cruise will be the 52nd recipient of the American Film Institute‘s prestigious life achievement award. The “Mission: Impossible” and “Digger” star will be feted with a gala tribute at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles on April 24.

“Tom Cruise is a global icon,” said AFI board of trustees chair Kathleen Kennedy wrote in a statement. “As an actor and producer, he brings an extraordinary commitment to everything he does. What I especially admire is his deep belief in movies and their ability to bring people together. That passion has made him an extraordinary ambassador for American film around the world. It is AFI’s honor to present him with the 52nd AFI Life Achievement Award.”

Related Stories
Why Seeing ‘Digger’ in VistaVision Could Change Your Mind About the Tom Cruise Box Office Flop
After the ‘Digger’ Disaster, What Should Tom Cruise Do Next?

Now 64 years old, Cruise has remained one of the industry’s most prominent stars since he launched in the 1980’s with leading roles in “Risky Business,” “Top Gun,” and “The Color of Money.” As the unshakably determined secret agent Ethan Hunt, he led the “Mission: Impossible” action series across 30 years, starring in eight entries and subjecting himself to increasingly daredevil stunt-work as they went along. Other blockbuster titles have included “Rain Man,” “A Few Good Men,” “Collateral,” “Edge of Tomorrow,” and “Interview with the Vampire.”

Cruise has also been nominated for three Oscars: in lead actor for 1989’s “Born on the Fourth of July” and 1996’s “Jerry Maguire,” and in supporting actor for 1999’s “Magnolia.” He was also an Academy Award nominee as a producer for 2022’s “Top Gun: Maverick,” which was nominated for best picture. In 2025, he received an honorary Oscar from the Academy at the organization’s annual Governor’s Awards.

The star also finds himself back in the awards conversation this year for his lead turn in Alejandro González Iñárritu’s “Digger.” Cruise will next be seen in the sequel “Days of Thunder 2.”

The Life Achievement Award is AFI’s highest honor recognizing a career in the film industry. John Ford was the first recipient in 1973, with other notable names including Orson Welles, Alfred Hitchcock, James Stewart, Steven Spielberg, Martin Scorsese, Jack Lemmon, Tom Hanks, Robert De Niro, Meryl Streep, Jane Fonda, and Diane Keaton. More recent honorees include Julia Andrews, Nicole Kidman, and Francis Ford Coppola.

This year’s ceremony honored Eddie Murphy, with a recording of the tribute later premiering on Netflix. The event included Bill Burr, Dave Chappelle, Arsenio Hall, Spike Lee, Mike Myers, Chris Rock, and Stevie Wonder among its presenters and performers.

entry.title: Neon Boards ‘NAZA’ to Expand Distribution for Documentary About Israel’s Military Strikes on Gaza
entry.summary: Neon will release "NAZA," a documentary about Israel's military strikes on Gaza from the "No Other Land" directors — self-distributed until now.
entry.content:
Neon has joined the release of “NAZA,” a documentary composed of anonymous interviews with 24 members of the Israeli military that details the country’s airstrikes on Gaza and the killing of Palestinian civilians.

The partnership marks a major sea change within the distribution market. Filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor‘s last documentary “No Other Land” (co-directed with Hamdan Ballal and Basel Adra), about Israeli settler violence in Palestine’s occupied West Bank, went without a U.S. distribution partner in 2024 — a development that, at the time, Abraham said he “read it as something that’s completely political.” Many in the industry have speculated that traditional distributors had concluded that documentaries about Israel and Palestine were too controversial to do business with in the U.S. Despite being released independently, “No Other Land” ended up grossing $3.6 million in theaters worldwide and won the Oscar for best documentary feature.

Related Stories
Audiences Want to See Documentaries About Gaza, Israel, and Palestine — Why Are Distributors Still Scared?
Box Office: ‘NAZA,’ Documentary About Israel’s Attacks on Gaza That Was Too Hot for Distributors, Crosses $500,000

For the “NAZA” release partnership, Neon will “work with the filmmakers to expand its footprint and to reach larger audiences and communities.” More exact details on how the distributor will support the film are yet to be disclosed.

After premiering at Venice Film Festival, where it was embraced by critics and won the special jury prize, “NAZA” immediately set an independent theatrical release in the U.S. and abroad. After opening in the U.S. on September 30, the film passed a $500,000 gross less than two weeks into its plan to play 85 theaters across 30 cities. The newspaper The Guardian, which produced “NAZA,” is planning to make the feature available to stream its website for free in November.

“Yuval and Rachel have created one of the best films of the year; it’s an extraordinary work of art and eyewitness testimony that stands alongside landmark documentaries like Laura Poitras’ ‘Citizenfour’ and Joshua Oppenheimer’s ‘The Act of Killing,'” reads a statement from Neon. “At the heart of Neon’s mission is a commitment to championing the best cinema from around the world. We’re proud to join the incredible team already working on the film and help bring it to the widest audience possible.”

Prior to the Neon deal, “NAZA” had already secured distribution plans across 50 countries. The film is produced by The Guardian with James Wilson’s JW Films banner, in association with Placeholder Films and Unseen Hand. “The Zone of Interest” director Jonathan Glazer is an executive producer. MK2 Films negotiated the deal with Neon.

entry.title: Japanese Cult Blockbuster ‘Rex: A Dinosaur’s Story’ to Get First U.S. Theatrical Release in December
entry.summary: "Rex: A Dinosaur Story" was one of the most expensive films ever made in Japan, but its release was cut short when its director was arrested.
entry.content:
Kani Releasing will bring the 1993 feature “Rex: A Dinosaur’s Story” stateside in December, setting its first-ever U.S. theatrical release. The Christmas-set comedy, which features animatronics by Italian effects guru and “E.T. the Extra Terrestrial” design creator Carlo Rambaldi, will receive a one-week run at New York’s independent theater Metrograph on December 11, with openings in Chicago, Seattle, Austin, and other markets to follow.

Released in Japan on July 3, 1993, “Rex” was heavily marketed and positioned to contend with the ranks of rival U.S. tentpoles. The blockbuster ambitions are best illustrated by the production’s recruitment of Rambaldi. The effects artist began his career in the Italian film industry, working filmmakers like Dario Argento and Mario Bava, before making a jump to Hollywood and contributing to productions like “Close Encounters of the Third Kind,” “Alien,” and “Dune.” “Rex” was certainly chasing the child-actor and animatronic two-hander dramatics of “E.T.,” which were made possible by Rambaldi’s work designing the character.

Related Stories
Watch Ava Duvernay Explain Why the 14th Amendment Is So Much More Than Birthright Citizenship
Gen Z Feels ‘Doomed’ Watching AI, but Gen Alpha Feels Differently

“Rex” was actually a strong box office draw in Japan, grossing 2.2 billion yen in its theatrical run to rank as the seventh-highest-grossing release of 1993. But at a production budget of 2 billion yen, the family film was still a money loser in theaters.

As Kani Releasing describes it, original distributor Shochiku also pulled “Rex” from theaters after the film’s then-dominant director Haruki Kadokawa was accused of instructing an aide to smuggle cocaine from the United States. Though the blockbuster director argued his innocence, he was convicted in 1994 and served a two-and-a-half year sentence. (Shortly after, he had managed to direct another feature: the 1997 adaptation of Yasutaka Tsutsui’s sci-fi novel “The Girl Who Leapt Through Time.”)

The North American release comes after Japan Society programmed a new remaster during its 2026 edition of New York’s Japan Cuts festival in July. Kani Releasing is handling distribution, adding to its catalogue of repertory titles and rising directors from Asian film industries.

“Rex: A Dinosaur’s Story” will play Metrograph to open its “Dinosauria” series. Running through January 3, other titles programmed include “Fantasia,” “Godzilla,” “Journey to the Beginning of Time,” “Jurassic Park,” “The Land Before Time,” and “The Tree of Life.”

entry.title: Watch Ava Duvernay Explain Why the 14th Amendment Is So Much More Than Birthright Citizenship
entry.summary: At IndieWire's Art of the Doc event, the '13th' director explained why her Netflix follow-up contained much more than she initially expected.
entry.content:
When Ava DuVernay approached Netflix about making a follow-up to “13th,” her acclaimed documentary about the legacy of the constitutional amendment that abolished slavery, she thought it was a fairly straightforward proposition. The 14th Amendment is best known for offering U.S. citizenship to everyone born in America, a right that is frequently attacked by the current administration.

That seemed like enough material for another film, but the two-year process of making “14th” taught her that the amendment contains so much more.

During a conversation with IndieWire’s Chris O’Falt at our Art of the Doc event in Los Angeles, DuVernay explained how the project evolved over time.

Related Stories
Gen Z Feels ‘Doomed’ Watching AI, but Gen Alpha Feels Differently
A New Australian Horror Import Imagines ‘Obsession’ from a Very Different Perspective

“I thought we were talking about birthright citizenship. That’s what I sold to Netflix,” DuVernay said with a laugh. “We worked on it for two years. The whole first year we were making a movie about birthright citizenship. And then we started seeing the other parts get attacked. The parts where I was like ‘This is too hard, I don’t want to focus on these other parts.’ But when we started to hear them coming up in those headlines, you couldn’t leave that out.”

The duo discussed how the constitutional amendment “flies under the radar” compared to more notable ones that everyone memorizes in history class, despite containing important protections like the Equal Protection Clause and the Due Process Clause.

“It does [fly under the radar],” she said. “Which is wild, because it holds in it the rights that we abide by.I didn’t realize the depth that was in the 14th amendment. One of our folks in the film says it’s a constitution in and of itself. I didn’t know that the 13th, 14th, and 15th truly created a new constitution that got clicked onto the first one.”

Ultimately, DuVernay hoped that making her documentary can help steer the conversation in a way that allows future generations to see the value of these legal protections that we were previously able to take for granted.

“It really comes to who gets to tell the story, and whose voice is the loudest,” she said. “That really becomes what history is. It’s the stories we tell each other.”

Watch the complete conversation with DuVernay in the video above.

National Geographic Documentary Films, part of a joint venture between The Walt Disney Company and the National Geographic Society, is committed to bringing the world premium, feature documentaries that cover timely, provocative and globally relevant stories from the very best documentary filmmakers. Its award-winning and critically acclaimed films reach 300 million people worldwide in 180 countries and 33 languages across the global National Geographic channels and direct-to-consumer platforms Disney+ and Hulu. Recent films include the Emmy-nominated winner of the IDA Award for Best Feature “The Tale of Silyan;” Oscar® and Peabody nominee “Sugarcane;” Oscar-nominated and Peabody Award winner “Bobi Wine: The People’s President;” Emmy Award winner “Lost In The Jungle;” Oscar- and BAFTA-nominated “Fire of Love;” Emmy and Peabody Award winner “The Territory;” BAFTA nominees “The Rescue” and “Becoming Cousteau;” and Oscar- and BAFTA winner “Free Solo.” For more information visit films.nationalgeographic.com, or find us on Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, and YouTube.

entry.title: Gen Z Feels ‘Doomed’ Watching AI, but Gen Alpha Feels Differently
entry.summary: Over 30 percent of young people feel either "doomed" or "scared" when watching AI content, but a study found notable differences in age groups.
entry.content:
One of the more inexplicably popular sources of AI slop today is “Fruit Love Island,” an AI-generated TikTok parody series in which anthropomorphized fruits with abs and cleavage flirt and mingle in 60-second ripoffs of “Love Island.” It is as mind-numbingly dumb as it sounds, and though TikTok started suppressing and demonetizing the videos due to being low quality AI, per the series’ own website blog posts, it persists and has tens of millions of views.

Suffice it to say, your teenager or pre-teen may very well have come across these videos or could easily be obsessed with them. But depending on just how old your teen is, their mileage may vary.

Related Stories
‘Sinner Supper Club,’ a Gay Mumblegore Ghost Story, Sells to Factory 25
Nathan Fielder Was Not Supposed to Be in ‘You Can See Everything’

A new study from UCLA and the Center for Scholars and Storytellers called “Rewrite This! How Gen Z and Gen Alpha are Redefining Modern Storytelling” showed that while a majority of young people actually view artificially generated content and stories positively, there is a noticeable shift in how they feel as today’s kids get older.

The study found that 53.8 percent of people between ages 10 and 24 described emotions of either “fascinated” or “excited,” while only 32.1 percent used the phrases “doomed” or “scared.” However, when asked to complete the sentence, “Watching a story with AI in it makes me feel…,” those who felt “doom” compared to “excitement” went up considerably as the survey participants aged up. 27.4 percent of 18-24 year olds used the emotion “doom” compared to just 9.7 percent of those aged 10-13 and 25.1 percent of those 14-18 years old. Nearly half of those between 10-13 felt “excitement” when watching AI content.

The study notes that many of the respondents’ feelings about AI come from AI-native videos they find on their social media feeds. “Fruit Love Island” was one such example, but turns out there are plenty of other examples of AI fruit littering TikTok. It also mentions brainrot memes like “tung tung tung sahur” (no clue) and AI soap operas via vertical, microdramas from ReelShort, DramaBox, Drama Wave, and Pocket Films.

This all feels significant because the narrative tends to be that Hollywood and tech companies are pushing AI even though a lot of people simply hate it and are even repulsed when they see endless amounts of slop on their feeds or in any sort of film or TV. But while the study doesn’t draw any grand conclusions, it suggests there might be a generation gap between Gen Z and the emerging Generation Alpha, who might feel differently and look more favorably at AI than other young people.

“I’d like to see AI portrayed in a balanced and realistic way, showing both its benefits and potential risks,” one 13-year-old polled for the study said. “It would be interesting to see AI helping people solve problems, learn new things, and improve everyday life while also exploring questions about trust, privacy, creativity, and human control.” Smart kid.

This is the fifth year of the study from UCLA and the Center for Scholars and Storytellers. Last year we covered the study with the takeaway that while many young people still love movies and series, many of them are not watching on TVs or in theaters themselves and instead are viewing through YouTube, on phones and laptops, or unconventionally on social media.

This year’s study touched on some of the same questions and found that more than half of young people still ranked “see a movie at the movie theater” as the top weekend activity with their friends if geography and money were not a constraint. But it also had some other new areas of study including what themes they most prefer to see depicted on screen (hopeful messages over partying and drinking), whether they want to see social media influencers in their movies and shows (surprisingly, no), and even if the movies did a good job depicting neurodivergence on screen (only 22.7 percent said “yes, most of the time”).

Find more from the study here.

entry.title: A New Australian Horror Import Imagines ‘Obsession’ from a Very Different Perspective
entry.summary: Film critic, author, and horror expert Alexandra Heller-Nicholas writes about taking her teenage son to see “The Only One."
entry.content:
Alexandra Heller-Nicholas is a multi-award-winning Australian film critic and the author of eleven books on cult, horror, and exploitation cinema, including the book “1000 Women in Horror,” which was adapted to a feature documentary for Shudder in 2026. In 2024, she appeared in Alexandre O. Philippe’s “Texas Chain Saw Massacre” legacy documentary “Chain Reactions” alongside Stephen King, Patton Oswalt, Karyn Kusama, and Takashi Miike, which won the Venice Classics Award for Best Documentary on Cinema at the Venice Film Festival.

“It’s like if ‘Obsession’ was from the perspective of the woman actually being obsessed over.”

Related Stories
‘Sinner Supper Club,’ a Gay Mumblegore Ghost Story, Sells to Factory 25
Nathan Fielder Was Not Supposed to Be in ‘You Can See Everything’

I have just left an advance screening of Michael Schwarz’s new horror film “The Only One” with my teenage son, and the conversation is taking a surprising turn than what I perhaps expected. “Why is it the woman’s problem if men are weird about them? Why is it her job to help them figure it out?”

I’ve written a bunch of books of cult, horror, and exploitation film criticism, including monographs on rape-revenge cinema (yikes!) and “1000 Women in Horror,” my 2020 book which was adapted into a documentary for the horror streaming service Shudder in 2025, directed by Canadian filmmaker Donna Davies. I love going to horror movies with my kid because I get to experience them through different eyes to my own. But I am always a little self-conscious that our post-movie discourse leaves me sounding a little preachy, a little didactic, and, well, a little… parental.

But this kid clearly does not need spoon-feeding and is fully equipped to figure things out by himself. Unlike most of the horror movies we see together, this screening is unusual because I am here largely in a civilian capacity. We weren’t here for the rigorous social analysis of contemporary horror, but rather for largely personal reasons: one of my oldest friends, Martyn Pedler, co-wrote the film with Marek Polgar.

Martyn and I moved to the south-eastern Australian city of Melbourne over thirty years ago from the nation’s tiny and exceedingly dull capital, Canberra. Gender politics aside, “The Only One” most immediately spoke to me of that palpable anxiety from being an adult returning home to the small town you outgrew. It’s “Welcome Home Roxy Carmichael” with a body count.

“The Only One” begins in Los Angeles, where Zoe (Mel Jarnson) is working as a barista to pay the rent when her dreams of superstardom remain acutely unfulfilled. Begrudgingly returning home to the small town she left with big dreams and a string of broken hearts trailing behind her, with the help of her best friend and the town’s token goth (Saphira Moran) — there’s always one — the two women face the growing realization that someone is killing off Zoe’s many exes, one by one. Dressed as a classically cartoonish Prince Charming no less, the killer slash-and-dices his way through a list of everyone Zoe dated at high school. In doing so, an array of future possible victims return to Zoe’s life – some for better, and some for worse.

Based on this brief synopsis alone, that some of these exes (most notably the truly repugnant local cop, played by Ben O’Toole) default to slut-shaming Zoe is as depressing as it is seemingly inevitable. Refreshingly, however, the film is unambiguous: this is creepy and wrong, a reflection of his flawed character, not hers.

While “The Only One” was in production long before Curry Barker’s “Obsession” was even released, it thus provides a flip side to the same conversation about gender, agency, and that age-old question: “Why are so many men just so damned weird about women who aren’t interested in them?”

While “The Only One” might have inadvertently stumbled into the same discursive terrain as one of the biggest surprise horror hits of recent years, its heritage can be traced back much earlier. From romance-themed horror films like George Mihalka’s “My Bloody Valentine” (1981) and the long-tail of gothic romantic literature from Bram Stoker’s “Dracula” (1897) to Stephanie Meyer’s “Twilight” novels, this century alone has seen a boom of horror-romances in the indie film space especially, with Justin Benson and Aaron Moorhead’s “Spring” (2014) and Jeremy Gardner and Christian Stella’s “After Midnight” (2019) surely at the top of the list.

When it comes to Australian horror, we punch well above our weight on this front. In 2025, Australian filmmaker Michael Shanks had a commercial and critical hit on his hands with the wholly singular body horror film “Together” with Dave Franco and Alison Brie. And sixteen years earlier, national horror hero Sean Byrne won hearts and minds at genre fests around the world with his deliciously twisted heartsick-aspiring-prom-queen-run-amok cult classic, “The Loved Ones.”

But “The Only One” continues the legacy of one film in particular. While the boom period of late ‘90s/early ‘00s teen slashers are linked most immediately to multiplex blockbusters like the “Scream” and “I Know What You Did Last Summer” franchises, in an admittedly uncharacteristic display of patriotism my favorite deep cuts were made by Australian filmmakers: Geoffrey Wright’s “Cherry Falls” (1999) and Jamie Blanks’ “Urban Legend” (1998).

If “The Only One” has one true ancestor, however, it is Blanks’ latter slasher film “Valentine” (2001) with “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” star David Boreanaz. Both films are drenched with perverse subversions of romantic iconography to gleefully playful effect, right down to their respective Cupid and Prince Charming killer masks which look like they could have been crafted by the same person.

And while “The Only One” pulls no punches when it comes to being wholly Team Zoe as she contends with a steady stream of creepy, obsessive guys, the famously ambiguous ending of Blanks’ “Valentine” refuses to grant us with the neat happily ever after we initially think we might be getting.

“Valentine” and “The Only One” were made by different filmmakers at different times, but with Blanks’ unexpected death in March this year at only 54 years old, Schwarz’s film feels like an accidental homage to one of the best horror filmmakers this country has ever produced.

That younger audiences can readily identify how “The Only One” taps into the same ideas as “Obsession” underscores how the film is much more than the retro pastiche its early ’00s horror vibes might at first suggest. But at the same time, “The Only One” is very much a film that continues a successful tradition of Australian romance-themed horror, wearing its heart on its sleeve for the genre classics that came before it.

“The Only One” world premiered at MONSTER Fest and will have its international premiere at the 2026 SOHO Horror Film Festival in the UK next month.

entry.title: ‘Sinner Supper Club,’ a Gay Mumblegore Ghost Story, Sells to Factory 25
entry.summary: 'Sinner Supper Club,' a gay mumblegore ghost story shot on an iPhone, has sold to Factory 25.
entry.content:
Factory 25, a Brooklyn-based independent film distribution company, has acquired worldwide rights to Daisy Rosato and Nora Kaye’s first feature film “Sinner Supper Club” at the New York premiere of the film at NewFest. The film is described as a “gay mumblegore ghost story” about friends reuniting to throw a “wake” for Genevieve, who has been priced out of New York City. As the night progresses and a heatwave traps them together, their long-ignored problems boil over….and then their dead friend shows up.

The film was shot in six days on an iPhone through improvisation. It is an homage to the scrappy and experimental filmmaking that characterized both the mumblegore and Dogme 95 movements. As part of production, the filmmakers wrote a manifesto, one that explored what it means to make a film in the 2020’s, with characters that represent the queer and transgender and gender nonconforming community.

Related Stories
Nathan Fielder Was Not Supposed to Be in ‘You Can See Everything’
$1 Million Box Office Haul for ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’ Provides a Release Template for the Smallest of Indies

The cast includes Elise Kibler, Ashil Lee, Genevieve Simon, Jayae Riley Jr., Sophie Sagan-Gutherz, Kaye and Rosato. In addition to directing and appearing in the film, Kaye and Rosato wrote the screenplay. Rosato also served as the cinematographer.

Factory 25 is planning a spring 2027 theatrical release followed by a digital and Blu-ray release. Factory 25 has released such films as “Funny Ha Ha,” “Ham on Rye,” “Happer’s Comet,” “Actual People,” “This Closeness,” “Family Portrait,” and “Queens of the Qing Dynasty.”

NewFest was founded in 1988 in response to the AIDS crisis. The New York LGBTQ+ Film Festival has been a tentpole of NYC’s queer cultural scene. In the subsequent years, NewFest has expanded into a film and media organization with year-long programs to serve all facets of the LGBTQ+ community.

entry.title: Nathan Fielder Was Not Supposed to Be in ‘You Can See Everything’
entry.summary: Lance Oppenheim on how the documentary changed course, including Fielder deciding to co-direct, appear on camera, and alter how it was shot.
entry.content:
“You Can See Everything” came together very quickly. Co-directors Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder came aboard the documentary project just weeks before its subject, Elizabeth Holmes, was scheduled to report to the Federal Prison Camp in Bryant, Texas, to serve an 11-year sentence for defrauding her Theranos investors.

While, as IndieWire previously reported, Fielder was deeply skeptical there was a film to be made with Holmes and her partner Billy Evans. (He even negotiated a “kill switch” in his deal with A24, permitting him to abandon the project at any point.) From the start, however, he did see it as an opportunity to collaborate with Oppenheim — not unlike what he did with Benny Safdie on “The Curse” — a director with his own distinct approach to capturing reality.

Related Stories
$1 Million Box Office Haul for ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’ Provides a Release Template for the Smallest of Indies
‘Fatherland’ Review: Pawel Pawlikowski Fans Will Feel Cozily, Coldly at Home with His Latest Tour Through Europe’s Regrets

“Nathan was very adamant from the jump with me, ‘I’m going to produce this, you’re going to direct this,’” said Oppenheim on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast. “And then he’s like, ‘I want to be there, though, and I want to see how you do it. I want to see how you work.’”

Oppenheim’s previous three nonfiction projects, “Some Kind of Heaven,” “Spermworld,” and the HBO series “Ren Faire,” were what the director describes as “docu-fantasies.”

“[In my previous three documentaries] I was interested in inhabiting a subjectivity and using a lot of cinematic tools and tricks of the trade to get an audience to care about the wants and needs and the obstacles for the participants I was working with in the film,” said Oppenheim.

The result is non-fiction projects that often look and feel like scripted narrative films, using the cinematic form expressively. (You can read more here about Oppenheim’s docu-fantasy approach on “Ren Faire.”)

“When we first got [to Holmes and Evans’ Del Mar beach cottage], I was very adamant, ‘Nathan, you know, I work in a very specific sort of way,’” said Oppenheim. “I work with one camera. I like to shoot anamorphically — it does something to the image and process that I like — and he was like, ‘OK, yeah, let’s try that.’

It’s a process that involves a small crew, four to six people maximum, with a preference for a specific and determined composition of a scene, rather than, like on most documentaries, covering the unfolding action with multiple cameras.

“Nathan hadn’t worked in this capacity in a really long time, maybe not since his short films in Canada,” said Oppenheim. He also noted arguably the biggest change for the “Nathan for You” and “The Rehearsal” creator: “He wasn’t planning to be on camera for this too.”

When it came to capturing Holmes and Evans in their beachside hideaway, the flaws of Oppenheim’s established approach became apparent right from the jump. “The anamorphic [lensing] lasted for about a day,” said Oppenheim. “We initially started with a wider aspect ratio. That wasn’t working. We realized that their life was extremely confined to this house because out of fear of paparazzi taking their pictures.”

Equally problematic was using only one camera, which Oppheim said “was a disaster” — a disaster Fielder, now perched behind the camera, picked up on immediately. “Every time Elizabeth and Billy would move our [camera] operators would struggle to catch up with them,” explained Oppenheim. “We weren’t shooting handheld, it was always on sticks [a tripod], so we’d have to switch lenses, or we’d have to throw a diopter on, and then we would miss the moment completely.”

It was during this stop and start process of needing to make camera adjustments, something interesting started to happen. “While the camera operators were changing things, Elizabeth and Billy would ask Nathan questions,” said Oppenheim. “And then the camera would come back on, [and] they’d continue asking Nathan questions. It felt like they were drawing Nathan almost in front of the camera, which was really interesting.”

According to Oppenheim, by the second day of filming, Fielder would start to appear on camera, but only in “fits and starts,” but as Fielder got pulled on screen with increasing frequency, “[Nathan said to me], ‘Actually, you know what? We should direct this together,'” he said. “And I was like, ‘Are you fucking kidding me? Of course. I want that, too.’”

As IndieWire has previously reported, Oppenheim, Fielder, and crew were befuddled early on by what they were observing — the couple’s behavior up-close only raised more questions, sparking disagreements among the filmmaking team of how to interpret what they were seeing (an experience audiences who have seen “You Can See Everything” are likely able to relate to). The filmmakers discovered they could probe and explore that confusion more fully with Fielder on camera.

“It was them pulling [Nathan] in, asking him questions, asking him his opinion on things, and then him also realizing, once that started happening, maybe there was an opportunity to at least bring up the things he was observing that were confusing to him, that were also confusing to us,” said Oppenheim. “Then once [Fielder started to appear more frequently on camera], we were like, ‘OK, we have to come up with a new system of doing stuff. This one camera approach doesn’t work.’”

Gone were the widescreen anamorphic lenses, as Oppenheim shifted to more standard documentary zoom lenses and a tighter 4:3 aspect ratio, which “[allowed us] to actually live in these moments on faces, which is seemingly what is most interesting to us right now, just seeing the nuances, the microexpressions,” said Oppenheim. “It also helps the environment change, so if we’re stuck in this house, [the tighter aspect ratio makes] it feel like maybe the space is a little bigger.”

Fielder insisted they needed multiple cameras in the beach cottage — there was too much going on, and capturing the small moments and micro-expressions between Evans, Holmes, and himself (and eventually Holmes’ parents) became vital to the project.

The solution was two camera operators, each on a zoom lens, shooting from different parts of the house for 14 to 16 hours a day. Because the cameras were often zoomed in on Holmes and Evans’ faces, Oppenheim worried they would miss the dynamics of the larger space, as well as moments when someone left the room. The solution was a third camera with a 12mm (extremely wide) lens, operated by Oppenheim himself.

According to Oppenheim, this significant shift in the approach to shooting the documentary, in conjunction with Fielder’s interaction with Holmes and Evans, allowed the “You Can See Everything” filmmaking team to find its rhythm.

“Once we were able to shoot for really long periods of time, it felt like both Elizabeth and Billy didn’t really — there was no pressure on a moment; it didn’t feel like we were doing something [akin] to a traditional interview. We were able to basically let their lives play out and follow almost everything without really knowing what we were interested in,” said Oppenheim. “And the lack of pressure on the moment made it so that Nathan was able to actually ask questions without [Holmes and Evans], as much as possible, [having] their guards up, and that was the real breakthrough.”

Oppenheim said his creative bond with Fielder, dating back to well before they considered making an Elizabeth Holmes film, was an interest “in the challenges of capturing authentic life.” Looking back, he thinks their solution to this challenge with Holmes required both filmmakers to step out of their respective approaches, because what was needed was “to bring the audience into that room, into the experience of being there.” Rather than creating a lens that heightened the subjectivity of the characters, or one of interpretation or humor, it was about inviting the audience to experience the “cognitive dissonance” they were having while observing the couple.

“For me it was a very different way of working, and for Nathan as well, I think. We had to sort of learn the language of each other, and in doing that, we were able to, I think, break new ground artistically,” said Oppenheim. “Essentially what we ended up creating is the most rigorous form of a vérité documentary that [Nathan] or I could have ever made, and what that entailed was really just being present, observing, trying to organically respond to things that jumped out at us at any given moment.”

To hear Lance Oppenheim’s full interview, subscribe to the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast on Apple, Spotify, or your favorite podcast platform. You can also watch the full interview on YouTube.

entry.title: $1 Million Box Office Haul for ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’ Provides a Release Template for the Smallest of Indies
entry.summary: Rich Spirit CEO James Shani talks about what led indie 'If I Go Will They Miss Me' to earning $1 million at the box office.
entry.content:
Before his film “If I Go Will They Miss Me” found a distributor, director Walter Thompson-Hernandez was already developing title treatments and ideas for marketing materials for how his film should be positioned. He had a clear sense of his audience and a foundation of followers in place, and it was important he worked with the right team to get the movie out there.

Now, months removed from its premiere in the NEXT section at Sundance 2026, “If I Go Will They Miss Me” has found a greater audience than perhaps the director or its distributor, Rich Spirit, ever imagined. The film has surpassed $1 million at the domestic box office over a span of five weeks in theaters, only going as wide as 251 screens. It opens digitally for PVOD rental on October 23, but the film has earned enough demand and word of mouth that it will remain in some independent theaters in limited release for longer.

Related Stories
‘Fatherland’ Review: Pawel Pawlikowski Fans Will Feel Cozily, Coldly at Home with His Latest Tour Through Europe’s Regrets
After ‘You Can See Everything,’ What’s Next for ‘The Rehearsal’?

James Shani, founder of Rich Spirit, said the film upon seeing it at Sundance was “undeniable” and had a clear audience with an African American-forward crowd that is often underserved by the box office. But it was existing in an environment where other companies weren’t taking the bet on these types of movies.

“I really believed that this story and this this movie was specific and nuanced, and what Walter and the team have made is something that takes stories and takes circumstances that aren’t painted with the traditional tropes,” Shani told IndieWire about the film’s box office success.

The film stars J. Alphonse Nicholson and Danielle Brooks and follows a 12-year-old boy trying to reconnect with his estranged father following a prison stint. So it’s a film about fatherhood and community, but it illustrates it with a few surreal turns and visions that have kept audiences attentive. Shani says that the film has really struck a chord with those who watch it, and he’s seen numerous TikToks of people in tears coming out of the theater begging people to see the film.

“The way that this story is crafted I think breaks people open in a way that they didn’t necessarily expect but then leaves them with some hope,” Shani said.

He believes that while the box office success has been great, the metrics of success for indies have to evolve. Rich Spirit’s internal figures suggest that over 5 million people have awareness of the film via social media, even if they’ve yet to see the film in theaters, and the film’s word of mouth and reach is a good sign for its prospects on digital.

Earning $1 million at the box office for a movie of this size (“If I Go Will They Miss Me” had a P&A spend well below $1 million), is in a post-COVID era becoming akin to some studio films surpassing $100 million at the box office. We’re far removed from the days when Sundance movies like “Little Miss Sunshine” or “Napoleon Dynamite” were cleaning up at the box office, and the big sales for the most part have been via streamers that aren’t releasing these tiny indies in theaters. Those that do find homes, which hasn’t been many in recent festivals, aren’t even putting up these numbers.

“Union County,” one of the U.S. Dramatic competition titles this year and starred Will Poulter and Noah Centineo, was released by Oscilloscope this summer and made only $190K at the box office. Rob Lowe fim “The Musical,” also a competition title, did $224K from Blue Harbor Entertainment. “The Incomer” with Domhnall Gleeson and which also premiered in NEXT, did surpass $1 million, but only thanks to a huge showing in the UK, and it made only $209K domestic.

Shani comped “If I Go” to another Sundance title, “Exhibiting Forgiveness,” which shared a similar audience and also played in theaters throughout October for roughly five weeks in 2024. That film from Roadside Attractions opened on over 700 theaters but only took in about half, $506K, of what “If I Go” has already earned.

In order to make the most of the screens they had, Rich Spirit first opened on just a single screen in Los Angeles and opened to $39K, a strong per-screen-average. It then ballooned with an additional $336K in its second weekend. The film was shot in LA and the city acts as something of a character in the story, so it was important to keep the film rooted here as well, getting the chance to play at a few art houses but also the major AMC Century City, and the film saw a healthy split of revenue from both indie venues and the big chains.

But they also executed on what Rich Spirit internally called the Obama Strategy. They targeted some Black communities in Atlanta, Houston, Charlotte, Raleigh, and more that have been underserved by the box office and are still playing in some of those markets. And because Thompson-Hernandez already has an established audience as a noted journalist and photographer, they’ve been able to lean into his audience that was already there. It’s a model that other indies have tried but with some mixed results.

For Rich Spirit, this is just the upstart distributor’s third title, which also includes “BLKNWS: Terms and Conditions” and “The Apprentice,” the Donald Trump biopic which Shani salvaged and released under far different circumstances than how “If I Go Will They Miss Me” has been approached. Shani will be crawling this upcoming Sundance again to find another similar title it can champion in the same way.

The key now is to find ways to continue to serve that audience on PVOD, including developing a merchandising strategy, and supporting Thompson-Hernandez on his next step.

“To me, this is a a first feature that, if we could do our job well enough, sets Walter off to do whatever he wants to do next. And I think he’s already doing that,” Shani said.

entry.title: ‘Fatherland’ Review: Pawel Pawlikowski Fans Will Feel Cozily, Coldly at Home with His Latest Tour Through Europe’s Regrets
entry.summary: Sandra Hüller stars in Pawel Pawlikowski's crispy drawn postwar portrait 'Fatherland' as German author Thomas Mann's daughter. Review.
entry.content:
Editor’s Note: This review was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Mubi opens “Fatherland” in select theaters starting Friday, October 23.

The aching black-and-white, the Academy aspect ratio, the streak of fatalism running between dueling identities — you know when you’re in a Pawel Pawlikowski movie. His latest, “Fatherland,” takes us on a melancholy road trip from U.S.-operated Frankfurt to Soviet-run Weimar in Germany with “The Magic Mountain” author Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler) and his daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller) in 1949.

About as sentimental as any film by the Polish auteur gets — which is to say not at all, despite one long-delayed tear finally shed — it’s another austere, rigorously crafted odyssey through European postwar regret. Stylistically aligned with “Ida” and “Cold War” to perhaps complete a loose trilogy, “Fatherland” opens an intentionally narrow window onto the strained relationship between Mann and Erika after his 16 years of exile in the United States. Pawlikowski’s elliptical style — keen on empty spaces, minimal dialogue, and crisp cutting — has its limits in terms of achieving an emotional payoff, but the actors’ understated turns make for a captivating (and, at 82 minutes, miraculously short) elegy to a lost homeland at the kickoff of the Cold War.

Related Stories
After ‘You Can See Everything,’ What’s Next for ‘The Rehearsal’?
‘Possible Love’ Trailer: Two Families Are Divided by a Documentary in Netflix Oscar Hopeful

“Fatherland” begins in, of all places, Cannes, a glamorous swath of coastal cityscape that is about as far a cry as you can get from the postwar ruinousness happening in Germany, north of France. That’s where Klaus Mann (August Diehl), Thomas’ homosexual Communist son, would end up taking his own life, but a furtive phone call between twin brother and sister reveals both their closeness as well as the fractures in a broken family dynamic. Erika is living in the Palisades with her father, working as his assistant, when he is summoned back to Germany for the first time since he left his home country in 1933, strongly opposed to Nazi dictatorship. He’s due to receive the Goethe prize, a symbol of lasting German culture amid a country now divided between East and West and scrambling to retain its now-stained identity.

The road trip beginning in Frankfurt and ending in Weimar, where a celebration of Goethe’s 200th birthday is set to take place, becomes the setting for father and daughter to perhaps ease the strains in their relationship. Hüller plays Erika as a kind of doting clerk who has spent more than a decade defending his reputation against accusations of Communism and more (Mann was also, like his son, understood to be homosexual, though this film doesn’t dig into that aspect of the “Death in Venice” author’s life). But there’s also simmering resentment, which starts to quietly boil over once they learn terrible news about Klaus. What about her own life, as more than just somebody’s daughter? (Erika had a rich career as a writer and war correspondent, but that’s for another film.)

“Let’s go home,” Erika says at one point to her father on their journey. “Where is that?,” he says. Indeed, Zischler’s Mann is a lost soul, and these two, to quote Nick Cave, are a bit “like two lost suitcases on a carousel going nowhere.” Fans of Pawlikowski’s style will feel coldly, cozily at home in how their emotionally stingy relationship plays out. There’s also a kind of, to use a crass comparison, “Midnight in Paris” of burned-out revolutionaries and period famous types that rolls out as they brush up against various public figures on their trip. That includes a terse run-in with her bitter Nazi husband Gustaf Gründgens (at this point in time she’s now married to poet W.H. Auden, as the script conspicuously points out) at a fancy cocktail party, and a car ride with German Communist author Johannes R. Becher (Devid Striesow).

Erika also definitely has a sapphic frisson with Associated Press journalist Betty Knox (Anna Madeley), who is in attendance at the press conference that opens the Manns’ Eurotour. Pawlikowski loyalists will also appreciate a cameo from “Cold War” star Joanna Kulig (who in that film was playing a version of the filmmaker’s mother) as a lounge singer.

Shooting Poland for Germany, Pawlikowski’s regular cinematographer Łukasz Żal follows the Manns’ black Buick through a haunted, guilt-ridden Germany from a characteristically chilly remove. That Pawlikowski is telling a story of actual historical figures proves a fascinating challenge for a filmmaker who has previously invented characters to serve as historical reminders.

But that also means that he doesn’t quite psychologically penetrate either of the Manns as immersively as his previous work. Hüller’s performance is typically strong and rooted in cold stares and silences, adding to an already amazing year for the German actress between achieving blockbuster exposure in “Project Hail Mary” and winning the Berlinale best actress prize for her performance in another black-and-white period drama, “Rose.” Stacked against those turns, though, this may not be the role she’ll be best remembered for this year, even as her performance is as masterful and airtight as ever.

What exactly the endgame of this road trip is doesn’t quite crystallize onscreen, leaving gaps and missing bookends that might encourage you to brush up on your European postwar history. To chisel a movie aesthetically within an inch of its life sometimes means the life inside gets lost in the process — though the Manns’ stopover in Soviet-occupied Weimar includes a briefly harrowing reminder of the Russian prisons happening next door to conference rooms and banquet halls in which socialism has begun to install itself. Pawlikowski is always best working in a more personal register, but “Fatherland,” even stripped of historical context, does finally end on a poignant grace note of healing between a father and his daughter.  

Grade: B

“Fatherland” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI opens it in select theaters starting Friday, October 23.

entry.title: After ‘You Can See Everything,’ What’s Next for ‘The Rehearsal’?
entry.summary: All that Nathan Fielder has done in his career, and especially in "The Rehearsal," has prepared him for what happens in "You Can See Everything"
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: The following article contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything.”]

If cinematographer David Bolen and camera operator Jonathan Mitchell were filming verité coverage of the IndieWire office in New York after the release of Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder‘s “You Can See Everything,” there would have been a similar visual sense of transience — a latent, unsettling tension of the kind that characterizes the first half of the A24 film, where Oppenheim, Fielder, and their small team were documenting Elizabeth Holmes’ last month of freedom before reporting to prison to serve her sentence for multiple counts of fraud.

Related Stories
‘Possible Love’ Trailer: Two Families Are Divided by a Documentary in Netflix Oscar Hopeful
‘Wildwood’ Review: Laika’s Epic Stop-Motion Wonder Lacks the Magic of the Studio’s Best Movies

Mostly, this was because we’re moving to a different floor of the office, and there were a lot of cardboard boxes, abandoned Tupperware, and mystery mugs scattered about. But it was also because of the impact of “You Can See Everything” — our individual reactions to it on staff and the wider reactions that we were seeing around the Internet.

The latter led our stalwart TV Critic, Ben Travers, to pose a question: Given the weekend that Fielder just had with “You Can See Everything,” would the filmmaker be more or less keen on a third season of “The Rehearsal,” his HBO series which has allowed him to do everything from bring the recreation of a Brooklyn bar across state lines to fly a commercial airliner?

I, Craft Editor Sarah Shachat, will admit that I wasn’t thinking too rigorously when I said the words, “He’s already made Season 3. It’s this movie,” but they were out before I thought to stop them. And look, we know from HBO Head of Comedy Casey Bloys that “The Rehearsal” Season 3 is in the works. Reddit is already trying to sleuth out whether Nathan Fielder intends to release the Epstein files or successfully transit the Strait of Hormuz, or whatever he’s planning on doing; IndieWire doesn’t know any more than you do.

But certain aspects of “You Can See Everything” do take on a distinct light when considered in the shadow of what Fielder (and Oppenheim) have done before. There are also a number of ways in which it is the Pokémon evolution of their previous work — and in which specifically “The Rehearsal” prepared, if not Fielder himself, than his audience to roll with a self-reflexiveness so recursive that even Peter Watkins would be like, “Wait, they did what?”

One of the core draws of the first season of “The Rehearsal” was its intricate sets — the great Nate’s Lizard Lounge, of course, but also studio builds of apartments. and locations thorough dressed by the show’s art team. “The Rehearsal” teaches us how to see that everything we interact with is constructed. Spaces aren’t ever just real or fake. If they’re real, they’re recreated and repurposed, often more than once while Fielder and his laptop loom in the center. If they’re “faked” for the show, they’re often where the most interesting and emotional exploration among the participants takes place.

Contrast Kor’s introduction in Episode 1 of the show with Angela’s in Episode 2. We first see Kor in his actual home, and while it’s safe to assume that the scene of the New York teacher playing along with “Jeopardy!” was staged for the cameras, there’s still a sense that we’re observing his day-to-day reality. With Angela, we start mid-rehearsal, first with a wall of surveillance cameras that pulls back to reveal Fielder in the control room/video village alongside the production crew and two mothers of children who’ll be playing Angela’s faux son, Adam. We see the artifice first, the person second. That colors how we move through both stories and understand those people, and Fielder’s relationship with them.

The first season of “The Rehearsal” questions what kind of authenticity can come out of an artificial setup or environment, especially for folks who have trouble expressing themselves. Maybe the artifice of “rehearsing” can lead to something good and genuine. The season becomes deeply concerned with the blurring of true emotion and performance — and how, for good and for ill, it’s much harder to draw a line between those things than it might seem. The question becomes even more fraught when it comes to child actors, where adults have a duty of care to try and keep reality straight for them while putting them in a situation where it starts to bend.

Here’s where the spoilers start — so seriously, don’t read unless you’ve already seen “You Can See Everything.”

When the “You Can See Everything” returns to the rental home in San Diego where Elizabeth Holmes and her boyfriend Billy Evans spent their last few months before moving down to Texas to comply with Holmes’ prison sentence, Nathan Fielder and Amanda Seyfried are looking for a grounding in the details of the space Holmes is no longer in, obviously. They’re also looking to bend reality far enough into artifice that they may actually be able to come back around to some truth. If Fielder and Oppenheim can run back the baffling month they spent in Del Mar through the scenes with Seyfried (as well as a game Christopher Abbott), maybe they can finally understand it, and Holmes.

There’s still some of those nearly invisible touches to it, though. Seyfried finds the now infamous bowl for beating eggs in the cabinet where it’s been the whole time, but when the film cuts to the recreate of Seyfried-as-Holmes and Fielder (as himself) meeting for the first time, a set decoration team has made the house look lived-in again. The rhythmic back-and-forth between the script that Fielder and Seyfried perform and the two of them discussing that scene as Fielder’s memory of a real event is also an intentional grounding of how we interpret what we’re seeing.

That first recreation starts with Fielder and Seyfried’s conversation, cuts to the recreation itself, and continues with Fielder talking to the Seyfried in a makeup chair, getting dressed for the role. The verite footage, conversation within a staged setting, and full recreation all exist on a spectrum of reality, one of that “You Can See Everything” is very careful to guide us through with the goal of helping us come to some conclusion (or grapple with our inability to draw one). It’s similar arc just in that one sequence to the full first season of “The Rehearsal.”

In other words, Nathan and editor Adam Locke-Norton learned it from watching Nathan.

They learned even more from Season 2 of “The Rehearsal,” which grapples with the struggle for any one of us to be able to successfully communicate to another person, even when the stakes are life and death. The first episode of Season 2 goes into this in depth, but one only needs to watch the painful interview CNN did with Fielder about the show to see how easy it is for people to dismiss anything said by a comedian, even some extremely saliant points about the safety that rides on good communication between pilots in the cockpit, and how it is in desperate need of improvement.

Beyond that dilemma, the extent to which any of us can successfully understand each other is at issue in both “You Can See Everything” and “The Rehearsal” Season 2. The HBO show does a fantastic job of exploring the pressures and incentives, implicit and explicit, that prevent pilots from communicating better. The recreations in Season 2, be they of a fully functional airport terminal or Fielder embodying Sully Sullenberg for “the miracle on the Hudson” after speed-running thorugh playing the pilot’s entire life, are in service of explicating and exploring those communication hangups — with cheeky a little bit of Evanessance thrown in, too.

The recreations in “You Can See Everything” are about trying to create a fuller picture of imperfect communication to fully understand the extent to which it’s genuine or not. It is a fascinating inverse of Season 2 of “The Rehearsal,” where Fielder actually becomes a pilot rated to fly a 737 and does so, on camera, carrying the entire extended cast of actors that have participated in Season 2 for the finale of the season. Fielder becomes his subject not just within the frame of the show itself, but in his lived experience, and that transformation has an impact on how he thinks about himself.

Grappling with the potential of seeing Holmes in prison but not being able to film or record the conversation in any way, Fielder talks it through with Seyfried. The actor is willing to recreate whatever Fielder needs. But Fielder isn’t sure that even she can be fully accurate — that her performance really can give us a chance to judge what Holmes has to say.

Of course they do end up shooting the recreation, intercut with Fielder and Seyfried talking through the script he’s written up before a fireplace that’s lit so dramatically Hitchcock wishes he put it in “Vertigo.” But there are conscious choices made here beyond the choice to do it. The first section of the sequence, where Fielder arrives at the prison and waits in the visiting room for a long time before Holmes shows up, unfolds with normal coverage — wides, medium wides on Fielder, insert shots of the vending machines, and so on. When Seyfried-as-Holmes does enter the scene, she’s covered from the back, in wides, and we’re unable to see Seyfried’s face.

There is a corner of the multiverse where Oppenheim and Fielder stage the entire conversation between Fielder and Holmes that way. The filmmakers could’ve let key moments of what Holmes says fall on Seyfried-as-herself, reading the script, and let whatever “true” version of Holmes — her expressions, her bearing her chemistry with Fielder — there is to be had all live inside the audience’s mind. There is a version of this sequence that withholds Seyfried’s interpretation in the name of “truth.”

Instead, we see Seyfried give a performance that we can never know is fully accurate; but in moments where she says, as Holmes “I’m tired of having other people speak for me” sure feels true. It feels lived. “You Can See Everything” is the opposite of Season 2 of “The Rehearsal” as well as its cautionary escalation. The film shows how natural it can be to get lost inside of a transformative performance, and that however close to accuracy we can get, it is never close enough.

It is Seyfried herself, arguably the true heroine of the film, who points that out that the more time Fielder has spent with Holmes, the trickier it may be for him not to care about her, and for their relationship not to color what we see.

But as both “The Rehearsal” and “You Can See Everything” point out, time with each other is all we have.

“You Can See Everything” is now playing in theaters.
